heading: Setting · Ayodhyā and Kosala in the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa

items.label: City
items.title: The city on the Sarayū: wall, moat, gates and gardens
items.alt: Aerial reconstruction of Ayodhyā: a long walled city laid out on a regular grid beside the Sarayū river, with a moat, gateways, mango groves and gardens.
items.attested: Kosala lies on the bank of the Sarayū, and Ayodhyā was built by Manu (Rāmāyaṇa 1.5.5–6). The city is twelve yojanas long and three wide, with well-planned highways (1.5.7). It has gateways and archways, a deep, hard-to-cross moat and a great wall like a girdle, with mango groves and gardens around it, and it holds horses, elephants, cows, camels and donkeys (1.5.10–13). Its plan is like an aṣṭāpada game-board, on level ground, built so densely that no plot is left unused (1.5.16–17).
items.prescribed: The translation used renders 'sāla-mekhalā' as a fort-wall, where Griffith has a belt of sāl trees; the painting follows the wall. The size, twelve by three yojanas, is many miles and is not drawn to scale; only the long, narrow shape is kept.
items.conjecture: The verses give no building material for the wall, so its brick, crenellations and corner towers are the painter's. The number and form of the gates, the bridges, the sailing boats on the river and the orange pennants are not in the text. The roofs and the form of the larger palaces are not described either. Colour: the text gives white only for the houses of the royal road and the tall palace buildings (2.17.2, 2.17.18) and, as Bharata's comparison, for the city seen from afar (2.71.19); the painter made nearly all the houses white.
items.note: Hypothetical reconstruction of a place in a poem, painted with an AI image model from the verses cited; the Rāmāyaṇa describes no excavated site. Figures, dress and architecture are illustrative; items marked Conjecture are not in the text.

items.label: Gate
items.title: A city gate: tribute, trade and craftsmen
items.alt: A fortified gateway of ancient Ayodhyā with a crowded forecourt of merchants, envoys, craftsmen, dancers and drummers, and elephants, camels and horses.
items.attested: The city is ringed with gateways and archways and has well-planned shop-fronts inside (1.5.10). It holds craftsmen and all kinds of machines and weapons (1.5.10), crowds of bards and eulogists, bastions with flags (1.5.11), troupes of dancers and actors (1.5.12), provincial kings bringing dues and traders from many countries (1.5.14), and the sound of great drums, mṛdaṅgas and vīṇās (1.5.18). Thousands of skilled archers and chariot-warriors live there (1.5.20–22).
items.prescribed: Verse 1.5.11 also names the śataghnī, which the translation calls a 'cannon'. It is a weapon of uncertain form and is not painted.
items.conjecture: The carved stone gate-towers with relief elephants, the wooden pavilions on top, the sun-emblem flags, the forge and sword stalls, the pack-camels and the dancers' stitched costumes are the painter's. The text does not say what the gate was built of or how it looked.

items.label: Royal road
items.title: The royal road, watered and strewn with flowers
items.alt: A wide clean street in ancient Ayodhyā, wet and strewn with flowers, with shops of cloth, flowers and perfumes and white multi-storey houses.
items.attested: The great royal road is straight, well laid out and always sprinkled with water, with scattered flowers (1.5.8). It is clean, perfumed with aloe incense and lined with white houses like clouds (2.17.1–2). It holds heaps of sandal, aloe-wood, silk and linen cloth, unpierced pearls, crystal, flowers and eatables (2.17.3–5). At every crossroads offerings of curd, unbroken rice, ghee, parched grain, incense and garlands are laid (2.17.6). Elephants, horses and chariots move along it, and people gather at the junctions (2.16.47).
items.prescribed: The verses say the offerings are laid at all crossroads; the painting shows one.
items.conjecture: The paving stone, the cloth awnings, the balconies with creepers, the carved pillar and the carts are not in the verses. The houses are white as the text says, but their storeys, balconies and ornament are the painter's. Dress and jewellery are conjecture. Colour: the verses call the houses along this road pale-white like clouds (pāṇḍura, 2.17.2); that is the only colour given.

items.label: Festival day
items.title: The city decked for the coronation, at dawn
items.alt: Ayodhyā at dawn decorated with banners, with dancers, drummers and crowds on a flower-strewn street.
items.attested: Before sunrise the citizens decorate the town (2.6.10). Tall banners and coloured flags are raised on temples that look like the silver lining of a cloud, at crossroads, in streets, on the big trees of temple compounds, on watchtowers of the city gates, on merchants' shops, on the houses of the rich, on all assembly halls and on conspicuous trees (2.6.11–13). Actors, dancers and singers perform on all sides (2.6.14). Children play at house gateways and talk of the coronation (2.6.15–16). The royal road is strewn with flowers and perfumed with incense (2.6.17).
items.prescribed: The comparison of temple tops with 'the lining of a cloud' gives a colour and a height, not a form.
items.conjecture: The conical white temple spires, the pointed gate arch, the balconies, the dancers' stitched skirts and blouses and the colours of the banners are the painter's. The text gives no shape for the temples. Colour: only the temple tops are given a colour, like the lining of a white cloud (2.6.11); the white houses and pale paving are the painter's.

items.label: Night of lamps
items.title: Night: lamps in the shape of trees
items.alt: Night in Ayodhyā, a street full of people lit by tall lamps shaped like trees, under a full moon.
items.attested: Fearing night would fall before the day's rites ended, the citizens set up lamps in the shape of trees to light all the streets (2.6.18). The road is strewn with flowers and incense (2.6.17). Villagers from every direction fill the city to see the ceremony (2.6.25–26), and the noise is like the roaring sea on a full-moon night (2.6.27–28).
items.prescribed: No second source is used for this scene.
items.conjecture: The golden branching lamp-stands, the royal chariot and elephants in the street, the sun-emblem banners and the flat-roofed terraces are the painter's. The verse says only 'lamps in the shape of trees'. The full moon is taken from the simile. Colour: the white terraces are the painter's; the verses give no colour for the houses.
items.note: Hypothetical reconstruction of a place in a poem, painted with an AI image model from the verses cited; the Rāmāyaṇa describes no excavated site. Figures, dress and architecture are illustrative; items marked Conjecture are not in the text.

items.label: Preparations
items.title: The coronation things laid out
items.alt: At dawn near the palace the coronation articles are laid out: golden pots, a throne, a tiger-skin chariot, a white umbrella, a white bull, a white horse and an elephant.
items.attested: Brahmans skilled in the Vedas wait with the priest Vasiṣṭha; ministers, army chiefs and leading citizens gather (2.15.1–2). The things prepared are golden pots, a decorated throne, a chariot covered with tiger skin (2.15.4), water from the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā and from many rivers and seas (2.15.5–6), gold and silver pots with parched grain, leaves, lotuses and water-lilies (2.15.7), honey, curd, ghee, parched grain, kuśa grass, flowers and milk (2.15.8), a golden fly-whisk and a white umbrella like the moon (2.15.9–10), a white bull, a white horse and a mighty elephant (2.15.11), and musicians and bards (2.15.12). Kings from many countries wait with the crowd (2.15.13–16).
items.prescribed: The same verses (2.15.8, 2.15.12) name courtesans and eight auspicious maidens; the image filter refused them, so they are not shown.
items.conjecture: The placing of the objects on a plaza by a river, the rugs, the form of the throne, the dress of the priests and the setting sun are the painter's. The text says only 'a nearby place'.
items.note: Hypothetical reconstruction of a place in a poem, painted with an AI image model from the verses cited; the Rāmāyaṇa describes no excavated site. Figures, dress and architecture are illustrative; items marked Conjecture are not in the text.

items.label: Rāma's palace
items.title: Rāma's palace and the crowd at its gate
items.alt: A lofty palace with carved wolves, peacocks and deer, and crowds waiting with gifts, and a great elephant.
items.attested: Sumantra sees Rāma's palace, shining like a mountain peak and like Indra's palace (2.15.31). It has large doors and hundreds of raised seats, festoons of gems and coral over the doorways, pearls scattered about, the scent of sandal and aloe, cranes and peacocks calling, figures of wolves and other forms sculpted on it, and it is full of birds and deer, 'high as Meru' (2.15.32–45). Country people wait outside with gifts (2.15.46), and the elephant Śatruñjaya stands there (2.15.47). Hunchbacked servants and Kirāta attendants move about (2.15.32–40).
items.prescribed: No second source is used for this scene.
items.conjecture: The stepped, terraced mass of the palace, the white stone, the carved timber gate and the arrangement of courtyards are the painter's. The text gives height and ornament, not plan. The howdah on the elephant is not mentioned. Colour: the verses give no colour for Rāma's palace, only that it shines and is high; its white stone is the painter's.
items.note: Hypothetical reconstruction of a place in a poem, painted with an AI image model from the verses cited; the Rāmāyaṇa describes no excavated site. Figures, dress and architecture are illustrative; items marked Conjecture are not in the text.

items.label: Rāma's ride
items.title: Rāma rides to his father's palace
items.alt: Rāma stands in a tiger-skin chariot with Lakṣmaṇa holding an umbrella and whisk, among horsemen, elephants, musicians and women scattering flowers.
items.attested: Rāma mounts a chariot covered with tiger skin, decorated with gold and jewels (2.16.27–30). Lakṣmaṇa stands behind, holding an umbrella and a chāmara over him (2.16.32). Horsemen and soldiers on elephants follow (2.16.34); armoured men with swords and bows walk ahead announcing him (2.16.35). Musicians, bards and the roars of warriors are heard (2.16.36). Women in the upper porticoes and turrets of the palaces scatter flowers on him (2.16.37–42). On the way he sees the clean royal road with elephants, horses and chariots (2.16.47).
items.prescribed: The verses call Rāma 'dark' in complexion elsewhere (2.2.53, 'like a black lotus flower'); they never say blue.
items.conjecture: Rāma's blue skin is a later iconographic convention, not in the verse. The brass horns, the harness and the wheel type, the design of the balconies, and the crowd's clothing are the painter's. The chariot's horses are shown in white; the verse gives no colour.

items.label: Palace precincts
items.title: Daśaratha's palace: guards and enclosures
items.alt: Rāma walks through the gates of the royal palace past bowmen and aged attendants in orange, with a chariot behind.
items.attested: Rāma crosses three enclosures in his chariot, guarded by men with bows, and the other two on foot, sending the crowd back (2.17.20–21). The palace blazes with radiance, with turrets like Mount Kailāsa and like clouds, tall white houses touching the sky, and royal houses called vardhamāna hung with nets of precious stones (2.17.17–19). In the inner quarters young men with darts and bows and polished ear-rings stand watch (2.16.1–2), and aged supervisors in orange clothes with canes stand at the doors (2.16.3).
items.prescribed: No second source is used for this scene.
items.conjecture: The marble floor, the gilt and jewelled gate frames, the layout of the enclosures and the distant domed roofs are the painter's. The domes are not in the text, which gives turrets and houses; they are an error of the image. Only the number of enclosures (five) is stated. Colour: the towers are called white like heavenly cars (pāṇḍura, 2.17.18); the white-and-gold marble floor and gate frames are the painter's.
items.note: Hypothetical reconstruction of a place in a poem, painted with an AI image model from the verses cited; the Rāmāyaṇa describes no excavated site. Figures, dress and architecture are illustrative; items marked Conjecture are not in the text.

items.label: Inner court
items.title: The inner court of the palace: birds, bowers and gold
items.alt: A palace garden-court with peacocks, parrots, swans, flowering trees, a well and seats of ivory, silver and gold.
items.attested: In Kaikeyī's apartments of the palace peacocks and parrots are kept, and curlews and swans are heard (2.10.12–16). There are bowers wound with creepers, champaka and aśoka trees, painted rooms, altars and fine seats of ivory, silver and gold, trees that give flowers and fruit in all seasons, wells in the middle, music, and short and hunchbacked attendants (2.10.12–16). Food and drink of many kinds is laid out (2.10.16).
items.prescribed: The original prompt for this scene was refused by the image filter because it centred on women. It was repainted as a garden court with attendants and the scene is about the setting, not the queen.
items.conjecture: The pool with lotuses, the courtyard's stone paving, the gilt table, the colour and form of the buildings and the particular musicians are the painter's. The wells appear as one pool; the text says wells. Colour: no colour is given for the walls or floors; the pale plaster is the painter's.
items.note: Hypothetical reconstruction of a place in a poem, painted with an AI image model from the verses cited; the Rāmāyaṇa describes no excavated site. Figures, dress and architecture are illustrative; items marked Conjecture are not in the text.

items.label: The silent city
items.title: Bharata comes home to a silent city
items.alt: An empty street in Ayodhyā at dawn with fallen leaves, closed doors, birds on rooftops and a chariot at the gate.
items.attested: Bharata reaches Ayodhyā at dawn after seven nights on the road and sees it from afar like a heap of white clay (2.71.17–19). He notes the parks are deserted, the trees along the road have lost their leaves, no one rides in or out, no sound of drums or vīṇās, no fragrance of aloe and sandal (2.71.21–29). He enters by the Vaijayanta gate and sees houses unswept with their doors open, no offerings or incense, temples deserted and without garlands, traders absent, birds clustered on temples and trees, and people weak, sad and tearful (2.71.33–44). Doors and hinges are rusted (2.71.46). Sumantra had found the same: no one greeting him, women at windows and in seven-storied mansions crying (2.59.10–16).
items.prescribed: The 'heap of white clay' is Bharata's comparison for the whitewashed look of the city from afar, not a description of the material.
items.conjecture: The pale stone paving, the particular carved door-frames, the cart with two horses, the vertical timber doors and the number of people are the painter's. Rust is not visible in the painting. The gate is shown as massive wooden doors. Colour: the whiteness comes from Bharata's comparison of the city to a heap of white clay (2.71.19); the pale street and walls are the painter's.
items.note: Hypothetical reconstruction of a place in a poem, painted with an AI image model from the verses cited; the Rāmāyaṇa describes no excavated site. Figures, dress and architecture are illustrative; items marked Conjecture are not in the text.

items.label: Entry into Ayodhyā
items.title: Rāma enters the city
items.alt: Rāma and his brothers in a splendid chariot among elephants, drummers, conch blowers, white cows and women carrying sweets.
items.attested: Sumantra yokes the chariot; Rāma mounts it (6.128.19–20, 6.128.27). Bharata takes the reins, Śatrughna holds the parasol, Lakṣmaṇa a fan and Vibhīṣaṇa a white whisk (6.128.28–29). Sugrīva rides the elephant Śatruñjaya and monkeys, in human form and ornaments, ride nine thousand elephants (6.128.31–32). Conches and kettle-drums sound (6.128.33). Musicians walk in front with cymbals and singing; men carry rice mixed with turmeric that shines gold, with cows, and maidens and brahmans with balls of sweets (6.128.37–38). The citizens raise flags on every house (6.128.42).
items.prescribed: The painting shows a few elephants, not nine thousand.
items.conjecture: Which of the brothers stands where, the style of the howdahs and the housefronts, and the dress of the women are the painter's. The chariot's gilded wheel and the number of horses are not in the verse.
items.note: Hypothetical reconstruction of a place in a poem, painted with an AI image model from the verses cited; the Rāmāyaṇa describes no excavated site. Figures, dress and architecture are illustrative; items marked Conjecture are not in the text.

items.label: Coronation
items.title: Rāma's consecration
items.alt: Rāma and Sītā are consecrated on a jewelled seat with gold pots of water; Hanumān kneels before Rāma, with vānara chiefs and a bear beside him.
items.attested: Vasiṣṭha seats Rāma with Sītā on a seat of precious stones (6.128.59). Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Kaśyapa, Kātyāyana, Suyajña, Gautama and Vijaya consecrate him with clear, fragrant water (6.128.60–61), and maidens, ministers, warriors and merchants sprinkle sap of herbs (6.128.62). The crown that Manu wore, made by Brahmā, is set on him on a throne of precious stones in the council-hall, studded with gold (6.128.64–67). Śatrughna holds the white parasol, Sugrīva a white whisk and Vibhīṣaṇa another (6.128.68–69). Sugrīva, Vibhīṣaṇa and the vānara chiefs are among those present at the consecration (6.128.84–87). The water was brought in jewelled jars from the four oceans and from five hundred rivers (6.128.49–57).
items.prescribed: No second source is used for this scene.
items.conjecture: Which figure is Hanumān, his kneeling pose and his monkey face are the painter's; the text says the vānaras took human form for the stay in Ayodhyā (6.127.43, 6.128.32) and gives no form for them at the ceremony. Rāma's dark complexion, the gold-pillared hall with its carved lions and the banners are the painter's. The number and posture of the sages, the ornament of the seat and the dress of the attendants are not in the text. The text does not describe the hall except as 'studded with gold'.

items.label: Kosala
items.title: The country around Ayodhyā
items.alt: Fields, tanks, cattle, a village festival and a roadside water-shed, with Ayodhyā in the distance.
items.attested: Rāma, asking Bharata whether he keeps the kingdom as it should be, describes a kingdom adorned with temples and with sheds where water is stored in tanks for travellers, with happy men and women, festivals and gatherings, well-tilled land, cattle free from cruelty, fields not fed by rain alone, free of beasts of prey and fear, and dotted with mines (2.100.43–46). Ayodhyā itself has fortified gates, elephants, horses and chariots, thousands of brahmans, warriors and merchants, and palaces of many shapes (2.100.40–42).
items.prescribed: This passage is Rāma's advice, a list of questions about what a good kingdom is like, not a description of Kosala at a moment in the story.
items.conjecture: The waterwheel, sailing boats, the quarry cranes, the thatched village houses and the temple pavilion are the painter's. The verses give the features in the list above and nothing of the layout.

items.label: Rāma's reign
items.title: The kingdom in Rāma's reign
items.alt: A green landscape of flowering trees and fruit, rain clouds, farmers, merchants, teachers and guards with Ayodhyā in the distance.
items.attested: In Rāma's reign there were no widows lamenting, no fear from wild animals or disease, no thieves or robbers (6.128.99–100). Trees flower and fruit regularly, free of pests; clouds rain in due time; the wind is pleasant to touch (6.128.104). The four classes do their own work, content and without greed (6.128.105). People talk of nothing but Rāma (6.128.103).
items.prescribed: This is the poem's closing praise of an ideal reign. It names no place, building or landscape, so the painting is a setting for the verses and not a record of any scene.
items.conjecture: The landscape, the city in the distance with domes, the teaching group, the farmers and guards and the market goods are the painter's, chosen to show the four classes at work. The text names no buildings. Colour: no colour is given.
